claim: Memory loss in Alzheimer's disease (AD) is attributed to pervasive weakening and loss of synapses.
source: Memory loss in Alzheimer's disease (AD) is attributed to pervasive weakening and loss of synapses.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that reflects established understanding in the field.

claim: Excitatory synapses on PV interneurons are dependent on the AMPA receptor subunit GluA4.
source: Excitatory synapses on PV interneurons are dependent on the AMPA receptor subunit GluA4, which is regulated by presynaptic expression of the synaptogenic immediate early gene NPTX2 by pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work and data presented in the manuscript.

claim: GluA4 is regulated by presynaptic expression of the synaptogenic immediate early gene NPTX2 by pyramidal neurons.
source: Excitatory synapses on PV interneurons are dependent on the AMPA receptor subunit GluA4, which is regulated by presynaptic expression of the synaptogenic immediate early gene NPTX2 by pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is supported by prior research cited in the manuscript and experimental data presented.

claim: In a mouse model of AD amyloidosis, Nptx2-/- results in reduced GluA4 expression.
source: In a mouse model of AD amyloidosis, Nptx2-/- results in reduced GluA4 expression, disrupted rhythmicity, and increased pyramidal neuron excitability.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: In a mouse model of AD amyloidosis, Nptx2-/- results in disrupted rhythmicity.
source: In a mouse model of AD amyloidosis, Nptx2-/- results in reduced GluA4 expression, disrupted rhythmicity, and increased pyramidal neuron excitability.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3.

claim: In a mouse model of AD amyloidosis, Nptx2-/- results in increased pyramidal neuron excitability.
source: In a mouse model of AD amyloidosis, Nptx2-/- results in reduced GluA4 expression, disrupted rhythmicity, and increased pyramidal neuron excitability.
evidence: This is inferred from the disrupted rhythmicity and hypersynchronous bursts observed in electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Postmortem human AD cortex shows profound reductions of NPTX2.
source: Postmortem human AD cortex shows profound reductions of NPTX2 and coordinate reductions of GluA4.
evidence: This is directly supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Postmortem human AD cortex shows coordinate reductions of GluA4.
source: Postmortem human AD cortex shows profound reductions of NPTX2 and coordinate reductions of GluA4.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 4 showing GluA4 reduction in AD brain.

claim: NPTX2 in human CSF is reduced in subjects with AD.
source: NPTX2 in human CSF is reduced in subjects with AD and shows robust correlations with cognitive performance and hippocampal volume.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and ELISA data shown in Figure 5.

claim: NPTX2 in human CSF shows robust correlations with cognitive performance.
source: NPTX2 in human CSF is reduced in subjects with AD and shows robust correlations with cognitive performance and hippocampal volume.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analyses shown in Figure 6 and Table 1.

claim: NPTX2 in human CSF shows robust correlations with hippocampal volume.
source: NPTX2 in human CSF is reduced in subjects with AD and shows robust correlations with cognitive performance and hippocampal volume.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6J.

claim: Amyloid Aβ that accumulates in human brain reduces excitatory synaptic function.
source: Amyloid Aß that accumulates in human brain reduces excitatory synaptic function (Shankar et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by Shankar et al., 2008.

claim: Mouse models of Aβ amyloidosis document that Aβ causes weakening and loss of excitatory synapses.
source: mouse models of Aß amyloidosis document that Aß causes weakening and loss of excitatory synapses (Kamenetz et al., 2003; Um et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Aβ increases pyramidal neuron excitability consequent to down-regulation of voltage sensitive ion channel Nav1.1 in PV inhibitory interneurons.
source: Aß also increases pyramidal neuron excitability consequent to down-regulation of voltage sensitive ion channel Nav1.1 in PV inhibitory interneurons (Verret et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by Verret et al., 2012.

claim: Human studies indicate amyloid accumulation typically precedes cognitive failure by many years.
source: However, human studies indicate amyloid accumulation typically precedes cognitive failure by many years (Jack and Holtzman, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Case studies report patients who were cognitively normal at death yet show pronounced Aβ plaque and neurofibrillary tangles consistent with AD.
source: Moreover, case studies report patients who were cognitively normal at death yet show pronounced Aß plaque and neurofibrillary tangles consistent with AD (Driscoll and Troncoso, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Mouse models of Aβ amyloidosis show cognitive improvement following inhibition of Aβ generating enzymes or amyloid reducing therapies.
source: Mouse models of Aß amyloidosis show cognitive improvement following inhibition of Aß generating enzymes or amyloid reducing therapies (Comery et al., 2005; Kimura et al., 2010; Townsend et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Similar successes to those in mouse models have not been reported in human trials for amyloid reducing therapies.
source: yet similar successes have not been reported in human trials.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of clinical trials, reflecting established knowledge in the field.

claim: NPTX2 is a member of a family of 'long' Neuronal Pentraxins that includes Neuronal Pentraxin 1 (NPTX1) and Neuronal Pentraxin Receptor (NPTXR).
source: NPTX2 is a member of a family of 'long' Neuronal Pentraxins that includes Neuronal Pentraxin 1 (NPTX1) and Neuronal Pentraxin Receptor (NPTXR).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the NPTX protein family.

claim: NPTX1, NPTX2 and NPTXR form disulfide-linked, mixed NPTX complexes that traffic to the extracellular surface at excitatory synapses.
source: NPTX1, NPTX2 and NPTXR form disulfide-linked, mixed NPTX complexes that traffic to the extracellular surface at excitatory synapses (Xu et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: NPTXs contribute to multiple forms of developmental and adult synaptic plasticity.
source: where they bind AMPA type glutamate receptors and contribute to multiple forms of developmental and adult synaptic plasticity (Chang et al., 2010; Cho et al., 2008; Gu et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2017; O'Brien et al., 2002, 1999; Pelkey et al., 2015, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: NPTXs directly bind AMPA type glutamate receptors.
source: NPTXs directly bind AMPA type glutamate receptors and can act in 'trans' as presynaptic factors that induce postsynaptic excitatory synapses (Lee et al., 2017; O'Brien et al., 2002, 1999; Sia et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: NPTXs can act in 'trans' as presynaptic factors that induce postsynaptic excitatory synapses.
source: NPTXs directly bind AMPA type glutamate receptors and can act in 'trans' as presynaptic factors that induce postsynaptic excitatory synapses (Lee et al., 2017; O'Brien et al., 2002, 1999; Sia et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: NPTX2 expressed by pyramidal neurons and secreted by axon terminals uniquely mediates activity-dependent strengthening of pyramidal neuron excitatory synapses on GABAergic PV-interneurons.
source: NPTX2 expressed by pyramidal neurons and secreted by axon terminals uniquely mediates activity-dependent strengthening of pyramidal neuron excitatory synapses on GABAergic PV-interneurons (Chang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Adaptive strengthening of the pyramidal neuron-PV interneuron synapse mediates homeostatic scaling of the circuit.
source: This adaptive strengthening of the pyramidal neuron-PV interneuron synapse mediates homeostatic scaling of the circuit, a process implicated in the ability of circuits to encode information (Turrigiano, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on homeostatic plasticity.

claim: Amyloidosis together with Nptx2-/- results in a synergistic reduction of inhibitory circuit function in conjunction with a reduction of the AMPA type glutamate receptor GluA4.
source: We examined the consequence of NPTX2 reduction in a mouse model of AD and found that amyloidosis together with Nptx2-/- results in a synergistic reduction of inhibitory circuit function in conjunction with a reduction of the AMPA type glutamate receptor GluA4.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: GluA4 is preferentially expressed in PV-interneurons at excitatory synapses where it co-localized with NPTX2 (presynaptic source).
source: GluA4 is preferentially expressed in PV-interneurons at excitatory synapses where it co-localized with NPTX2 (presynaptic source) (Chang et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and immunostaining data in Figure 4A.

claim: GluA4 confers rapid channel inactivation that is essential for fast spiking and contributions of PV interneurons to hippocampal circuit rhythmicity and memory.
source: and confers rapid channel inactivation (Angulo et al., 1997; Geiger et al., 1995) that is essential for fast spiking and contributions of PV interneurons to hippocampal circuit rhythmicity and memory (Fuchs et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: NTPX2 is required to bind and stabilize postsynaptic expression of GluA4 in PV-interneurons in conditions of altered activity.
source: Nptx2-/- dependent reduction of GluA4 was previously described in a different mouse model (Nptx2-/-; Nptxr-/-) where analysis suggested NTPX2 is required to bind and stabilize postsynaptic expression of GluA4 in PV-interneurons in conditions of altered activity (Pelkey et al., 2015, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In human brain GluA4 is selectively expressed in PV-INs.
source: In human brain GluA4 is also selectively expressed in PV-INs and is reduced in AD brain regions where levels correlate within samples to NPTX2.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data in Figure 4A.

claim: GluA4 is reduced in AD brain regions.
source: In human brain GluA4 is also selectively expressed in PV-INs and is reduced in AD brain regions where levels correlate within samples to NPTX2.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 4.

claim: GluA4 levels correlate within samples to NPTX2 in AD brain regions.
source: In human brain GluA4 is also selectively expressed in PV-INs and is reduced in AD brain regions where levels correlate within samples to NPTX2.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: NPTX2 is present in CSF.
source: To assess the relation between NPTX2 and cognitive function in human subjects, we determined that NPTX2 is present in CSF and levels are representative of brain NPTX2 since CSF NPTX2 discriminates clinically defined AD compared to age-matched controls.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and ELISA data in Figure 5.

claim: CSF NPTX2 levels are representative of brain NPTX2.
source: To assess the relation between NPTX2 and cognitive function in human subjects, we determined that NPTX2 is present in CSF and levels are representative of brain NPTX2 since CSF NPTX2 discriminates clinically defined AD compared to age-matched controls.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that CSF NPTX2 discriminates AD from controls, consistent with brain NPTX2 reduction.

claim: CSF NPTX2 discriminates clinically defined AD compared to age-matched controls.
source: To assess the relation between NPTX2 and cognitive function in human subjects, we determined that NPTX2 is present in CSF and levels are representative of brain NPTX2 since CSF NPTX2 discriminates clinically defined AD compared to age-matched controls.
evidence: This is supported by ROC analysis shown in Figure 5J.

claim: NPTX2 levels in AD subjects correlated with cognitive performance employing comprehensive psychometric tests including the Dementia Rating Scale.
source: Importantly, NPTX2 levels in AD subjects correlated with cognitive performance employing comprehensive psychometric tests including the Dementia Rating Scale, and surpassed the performance of other CSF markers including Aß42, tau and p-tau.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analyses shown in Figure 6 and Table 1.

claim: NPTX2 correlation with cognitive performance surpassed the performance of other CSF markers including Aβ42, tau and p-tau.
source: Importantly, NPTX2 levels in AD subjects correlated with cognitive performance employing comprehensive psychometric tests including the Dementia Rating Scale, and surpassed the performance of other CSF markers including Aß42, tau and p-tau.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of correlation analyses in Table 1.

claim: NPTX2 levels correlated with MRI measures of hippocampal volume.
source: NPTX2 levels also correlated with MRI measures of hippocampal volume, which is considered a marker of neurodegeneration and is linked to cognitive decline (Jack et al., 2010; Weiner et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6J.

claim: Hippocampal volume is considered a marker of neurodegeneration and is linked to cognitive decline.
source: NPTX2 levels also correlated with MRI measures of hippocampal volume, which is considered a marker of neurodegeneration and is linked to cognitive decline (Jack et al., 2010; Weiner et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: NPTX2 is not down-regulated in a widely used mouse amyloidosis model.
source: NPTX2 is not down-regulated in a widely used mouse amyloidosis model and is distinct from other CSF markers attributed to neurodegeneration including tau and p-tau in that NPTX2 is an indicator of specific rather than general excitatory synapses.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: NPTX2 is distinct from other CSF markers attributed to neurodegeneration including tau and p-tau in that NPTX2 is an indicator of specific rather than general excitatory synapses.
source: NPTX2 is not down-regulated in a widely used mouse amyloidosis model and is distinct from other CSF markers attributed to neurodegeneration including tau and p-tau in that NPTX2 is an indicator of specific rather than general excitatory synapses.
evidence: This is based on the known function of NPTX2 at pyramidal-PV interneuron synapses versus general synaptic markers.

claim: NPTX2 down-regulation results in disruption of pyramidal neuron-PV interneuron circuits that are important for brain rhythmicity and homeostasis of excitability.
source: Studies support the hypothesis that NPTX2 down-regulation results in disruption of pyramidal neuron-PV interneuron circuits that are important for brain rhythmicity and homeostasis of excitability, and represents a previously unrecognized mechanism important for human cognitive dysfunction and progression in AD.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 3 and prior work on NPTX2 function.

claim: NPTX2 down-regulation represents a previously unrecognized mechanism important for human cognitive dysfunction and progression in AD.
source: Studies support the hypothesis that NPTX2 down-regulation results in disruption of pyramidal neuron-PV interneuron circuits that are important for brain rhythmicity and homeostasis of excitability, and represents a previously unrecognized mechanism important for human cognitive dysfunction and progression in AD.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of evidence throughout the manuscript.

claim: NPTX2 protein was reduced in all cortical regions including those areas that display prominent classical neuropathological changes in AD, as well as areas that are typically less affected such as occipital cortex.
source: NPTX2 was reduced in all cortical regions including those areas that display prominent classical neuropathological changes in AD, as well as areas that are typically less affected such as occipital cortex.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Reductions of NPTX2 were evident whether referenced to actin or PSD95.
source: Reductions of NPTX2 were evident whether referenced to actin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) or PSD95 (Figure 1B); the latter indicating that NPTX2 down-regulation is distinct from a general reduction of excitatory synaptic markers.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: NPTX2 down-regulation is distinct from a general reduction of excitatory synaptic markers.
source: Reductions of NPTX2 were evident whether referenced to actin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) or PSD95 (Figure 1B); the latter indicating that NPTX2 down-regulation is distinct from a general reduction of excitatory synaptic markers.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that NPTX2 is reduced even when normalized to PSD95, a general excitatory synaptic marker.

claim: Nptx2 mRNA was prominently reduced in assayed regions of AD brain.
source: Nptx2 mRNA was also prominently reduced in assayed regions (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Neuronal Pentraxin 1 (NPTX1) and Neuronal Pentraxin Receptor (NPTXR) were not reduced in the same brain samples.
source: Neuronal Pentraxin 1 (NPTX1) and Neuronal Pentraxin Receptor (NPTXR) were not reduced in the same brain samples (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: Other IEGs including Arc and Egr-1 were not reduced in AD brain.
source: To further assess the specificity of NPTX2 down-regulation we determined that other IEGs including Arc and Egr-1 were not reduced (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: NPTX2 was not reduced in brain of subjects who were cognitively normal at death but whose brains exhibit pathology typical of AD including Aβ plaque and tangles [asymptomatic AD (ASYMAD) or preAD].
source: NPTX2 was not reduced in brain of subjects who were cognitively normal at death but whose brains exhibit pathology typical of AD including Aß plaque and tangles [asymptomatic AD (ASYMAD) or preAD (Codispoti et al., 2012; Driscoll et al., 2006; Driscoll and Troncoso, 2011) (Figure 1F and G, and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1F and G.

claim: Nptx2 protein and mRNA were reduced in middle frontal gyrus of Down syndrome (DS) subjects aged 19 y/o to 40 y/o compared to age matched controls.
source: Nptx2 protein and mRNA were also reduced in middle frontal gyrus of Down syndrome (DS) subjects aged 19 y/o to 40 y/o compared to age matched controls (Figure 1H to 1J and Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and qPCR data shown in Figure 1H-J.

claim: Nptx2 protein (normalized to actin) and mRNA were similarly reduced in older DS individuals with AD.
source: Nptx2 protein (normalized to actin) and mRNA were similarly reduced in older DS individuals with AD (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 1—source data 3).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Nptx2 transcription is regulated by methylation of flanking genomic sequences in pancreatic cells.
source: Nptx2 transcription is regulated by methylation of flanking genomic sequences in pancreatic cells (Zhang et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Nptx2 methylation assayed by pyrosequencing was low in human brain and not different between control and AD subjects.
source: however, Nptx2 methylation assayed by pyrosequencing was low in human brain and not different between control and AD subjects (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by pyrosequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nptx2 pre-mRNA expression was not different between control and AD subjects.
source: Furthermore, Nptx2 pre-mRNA expression was not different between control and AD subjects (Figure 2A) suggesting Nptx2 transcription is maintained in AD, and that reduced mRNA is consequent to reduced pre-mRNA processing (ex. splicing) or mRNA stability.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Nptx2 transcription is maintained in AD.
source: Furthermore, Nptx2 pre-mRNA expression was not different between control and AD subjects (Figure 2A) suggesting Nptx2 transcription is maintained in AD, and that reduced mRNA is consequent to reduced pre-mRNA processing (ex. splicing) or mRNA stability.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that pre-mRNA levels are preserved in AD.

claim: Reduced Nptx2 mRNA in AD is consequent to reduced pre-mRNA processing (ex. splicing) or mRNA stability.
source: Furthermore, Nptx2 pre-mRNA expression was not different between control and AD subjects (Figure 2A) suggesting Nptx2 transcription is maintained in AD, and that reduced mRNA is consequent to reduced pre-mRNA processing (ex. splicing) or mRNA stability.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that pre-mRNA is preserved but mature mRNA is reduced.

claim: miR-1271 was increased in AD frontal cortex.
source: We determined that miR-1271 as well as its originating pri-miR, pre-mRNA and mRNA [miR-1271 is generated from intron of human gene Arl10 (ADP-ribosylation factor-like 10)] were increased in AD frontal cortex where levels in individual samples correlated with Nptx2 mRNA (Figure 2C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: miR-1271 levels in individual samples correlated with Nptx2 mRNA in AD frontal cortex.
source: We determined that miR-1271 as well as its originating pri-miR, pre-mRNA and mRNA [miR-1271 is generated from intron of human gene Arl10 (ADP-ribosylation factor-like 10)] were increased in AD frontal cortex where levels in individual samples correlated with Nptx2 mRNA (Figure 2C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Analysis of AD precuneus gyrus detected similar preservation of Nptx2 pre-mRNA.
source: Analysis of AD precuneus gyrus detected similar preservation of Nptx2 pre-mRNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), and increases of pri-miR-1271, Arl10 pre-mRNA and mRNA, as well as increases of miR-182 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Analysis of AD precuneus gyrus detected increases of pri-miR-1271, Arl10 pre-mRNA and mRNA, as well as increases of miR-182.
source: Analysis of AD precuneus gyrus detected similar preservation of Nptx2 pre-mRNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), and increases of pri-miR-1271, Arl10 pre-mRNA and mRNA, as well as increases of miR-182 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Frontal cortex of DS cases showed up-regulation of the triploid miR-155.
source: For comparison, we examined frontal cortex of DS cases and confirmed up-regulation of the triploid miR-155 (positive control) together with increases in miR-96 and miR-182 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Frontal cortex of DS cases showed increases in miR-96 and miR-182.
source: For comparison, we examined frontal cortex of DS cases and confirmed up-regulation of the triploid miR-155 (positive control) together with increases in miR-96 and miR-182 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: miR-96, miR-182 and miR-1271 target the same sequence in Nptx2 3'UTR.
source: miR-96, miR-182 and miR-1271 target the same sequence in Nptx2 3'UTR (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 2E.

claim: All three miRs (miR-96, miR-182, miR-1271) reduce expression of a luciferase fusion encoding human Nptx2 3'UTR compared to a point mutant 3' UTR that prevents miR targeting.
source: We confirmed in heterologous cells that all three miRs reduce expression of a luciferase fusion encoding human Nptx2 3'UTR compared to a point mutant 3' UTR that prevents miR targeting (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E–F).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E-F.

claim: miRs expressed as pri-miRs by lentivirus in cultured mouse cortical neurons reduced native mouse NPTX2 protein expression.
source: miRs expressed as pri-miRs by lentivirus in cultured mouse cortical neurons reduced native mouse NPTX2 protein expression (Figure 2F to 2 H).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2F-H.

claim: miR-96 was most effective at reducing NPTX2 protein and additionally reduced Nptx2 mRNA but not pre-mRNA.
source: miR-96 was most effective and additionally reduced Nptx2 mRNA but not pre-mRNA.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and qPCR data shown in Figure 2F-H.

claim: NPTX2 is normally regulated by miRs that may mediate the prominent delay in up-regulation of NPTX2 protein.
source: We hypothesize that NPTX2 is normally regulated by miRs that may mediate the prominent delay in up-regulation of NPTX2 protein [for example after seizure (O'Brien et al., 1999), and that this process is dysregulated in AD and DS.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the miRNA data and prior observations of delayed NPTX2 upregulation.

claim: The miRNA regulatory process of NPTX2 is dysregulated in AD and DS.
source: We hypothesize that NPTX2 is normally regulated by miRs that may mediate the prominent delay in up-regulation of NPTX2 protein [for example after seizure (O'Brien et al., 1999), and that this process is dysregulated in AD and DS.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed upregulation of miRNAs targeting NPTX2 in AD and DS.

claim: NPTX2 is not reduced in brain of 6 month old APPswe/PS1∆E9 mice.
source: NPTX2 is not reduced in brain of 6 month old APPswe/PS1∆E9 mice (here termed hAPP) (Borchelt et al., 1997) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Amyloidosis in a similar mouse model increases hippocampal excitability by reducing excitability of PV-interneurons.
source: Amyloidosis in a similar mouse model increases hippocampal excitability by reducing excitability of PV-interneurons (Palop et al., 2007; Verret et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Spontaneous sharp wave ripples (SWR) were evident in all four groups (WT, Nptx2-/-, hAPP, hAPP/Nptx2-/-).
source: Spontaneous sharp wave ripples (SWR) were evident in all four groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–2D).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-D.

claim: SWR are spontaneous oscillatory currents that are dependent on PV-interneuron function.
source: SWR are spontaneous oscillatory currents that are dependent on PV-interneuron function (Csicsvari et al., 1999; Ellender et al., 2010) and reflect the near synchronous firing of pyramidal neuron ensembles.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: SWRs reflect the near synchronous firing of pyramidal neuron ensembles.
source: SWR are spontaneous oscillatory currents that are dependent on PV-interneuron function (Csicsvari et al., 1999; Ellender et al., 2010) and reflect the near synchronous firing of pyramidal neuron ensembles.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SWRs.

claim: SWRs occurred at a significantly higher incidence in hAPP/Nptx2-/- mice.
source: SWRs occurred at a significantly higher incidence, but with a lower peak frequency, in hAPP/Nptx2-/- mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E–2F).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E.

claim: SWRs occurred with a lower peak frequency in hAPP/Nptx2-/- mice.
source: SWRs occurred at a significantly higher incidence, but with a lower peak frequency, in hAPP/Nptx2-/- mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E–2F).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Gamma oscillations are field potentials recorded near the soma of pyramidal neurons and reflect the synchronized inhibitory currents created by PV interneuron synaptic drive.
source: Gamma oscillations are field potentials recorded near the soma of pyramidal neurons and reflect the synchronized inhibitory currents created by PV interneuron synaptic drive (Buzsáki and Wang, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In both WT and Nptx2-/- mice, gamma oscillations were observed with a peak frequency of 30 to 40 Hz.
source: In both WT and Nptx2-/- mice, gamma oscillations were observed with a peak frequency of 30 to 40 Hz (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: hAPP mice displayed a regular gamma-like rhythm, but at a lower frequency.
source: hAPP mice displayed a regular gamma-like rhythm, but at a lower frequency (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3C.

claim: hAPP/Nptx2-/- exhibited even slower 'gamma' oscillation with significantly reduced peak power.
source: hAPP/Nptx2-/- exhibited even slower 'gamma' oscillation with significantly reduced peak power (Figure 3D to 3F).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings and quantification shown in Figure 3D-F.

claim: Rhythmicity in hAPP/Nptx2-/- was disrupted by prominent hypersynchronous bursts indicative of increased network excitability.
source: Additionally, rhythmicity was disrupted by prominent hypersynchronous bursts (Figure 3D) indicative of increased network excitability.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3D and inferred from the nature of hypersynchronous bursts.

claim: NPTX2 is required for homeostatic up regulation of GluA4 at excitatory synapses on PV interneurons in response to increased pyramidal neuron activity.
source: NPTX2 is required for homeostatic up regulation of GluA4 at excitatory synapses on PV interneurons in response to increased pyramidal neuron activity (Chang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: GluA4 expression is not substantially altered in brain of NPTX2-/- mice.
source: GluA4 expression is not substantially altered in brain of NPTX2-/- mice (Figure 3G)
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: GluA4 is markedly reduced in Nptx2-/-/Nptxr-/- mice.
source: however, GluA4 is markedly reduced in Nptx2-/-/Nptxr-/- mice (Pelkey et al., 2015, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: NPTXR is required for mGluR-LTD.
source: Since NPTXR is required for mGluR-LTD (Cho et al., 2008), Nptxr-/- presumably increases pyramidal neuron excitability and demand for NPTX2 to bind and stabilize GluA4.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Nptxr-/- presumably increases pyramidal neuron excitability and demand for NPTX2 to bind and stabilize GluA4.
source: Since NPTXR is required for mGluR-LTD (Cho et al., 2008), Nptxr-/- presumably increases pyramidal neuron excitability and demand for NPTX2 to bind and stabilize GluA4.
evidence: This is inferred from the role of NPTXR in mGluR-LTD and the observed GluA4 reduction in double knockout mice.

claim: GluA4 was markedly reduced in hAPP/Nptx2-/- compared to WT control or hAPP.
source: We monitored GluA4 expression and found a marked reduction in hAPP/Nptx2-/- compared to WT control or hAPP (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Neither Nptx2-/- alone nor hAPP alone reduced GluA4 expression.
source: Neither Nptx2-/- alone (Figure 3G) (Pelkey et al., 2015, 2016) nor hAPP alone (Figure 3H) reduced GluA4 expression indicating that GluA4 reduction in hAPP/Nptx2-/- represents an emergent phenotype that impacts PV interneuron function.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3G and 3H.

claim: GluA4 reduction in hAPP/Nptx2-/- represents an emergent phenotype that impacts PV interneuron function.
source: Neither Nptx2-/- alone (Figure 3G) (Pelkey et al., 2015, 2016) nor hAPP alone (Figure 3H) reduced GluA4 expression indicating that GluA4 reduction in hAPP/Nptx2-/- represents an emergent phenotype that impacts PV interneuron function.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that GluA4 is only reduced when both conditions are present.

claim: GluA4 expression is selectively enriched in PV-interneurons in human brain.
source: As in mouse brain, GluA4 expression is selectively enriched in PV-interneurons in human brain (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: GluA4 expression was reduced in AD brain regions including precuneus and medial frontal gyri.
source: GluA4 expression was reduced in AD brain regions including precuneus and medial frontal gyri (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: The precuneus gyrus (Brodmann Area 7) resides in the parietal cortex and is part of the 'default network' with strong connections to the hippocampus.
source: The precuneus gyrus (Brodmann Area 7) resides in the parietal cortex and is part of the 'default network' with strong connections to the hippocampus (Buckner et al., 2008; Greicius et al., 2004; Vincent et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The precuneus is notable for high levels of amyloid detected by PET in AD subjects and some aged control individuals.
source: and is notable for high levels of amyloid detected by PET in AD subjects and some aged control individuals (Sperling et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The histopathology of the precuneus gyrus in AD is not different from surrounding brain regions.
source: The histopathology of the precuneus gyrus in AD is not different from surrounding brain regions (Nelson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: When GluA4 expression was evaluated separately in controls and AD subjects there was a strong correlation with NPTX2 expression in both groups, albeit levels of NPTX2 and GluA4 were lower in AD.
source: Interesting, when GluA4 expression was evaluated separately in controls and AD subjects there was a strong correlation with NPTX2 expression in both groups, albeit levels of NPTX2 and GluA4 were lower in AD (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In young adult brain GluA4 expression did not correlate with NPTX2.
source: In young adult brain GluA4 expression did not correlate with NPTX2 (Figure 4E and F)
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: NPTX2 expression was higher in young adult brain than in aged controls.
source: and NPTX2 expression was higher than in aged controls (Figure 4G and H, and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: NPTX2 expression is reduced with normal aging and becomes a determinant of GluA4 expression independent of overt cognitive disease.
source: These observations suggest that NPTX2 expression is reduced with normal aging and becomes a determinant of GluA4 expression independent of overt cognitive disease.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that NPTX2 and GluA4 correlate in aged controls but not in young adults, and NPTX2 is higher in young adults.

claim: GluA4 is further reduced in AD by NPTX2 down-regulation in the context of amyloidosis.
source: GluA4 is further reduced in AD by NPTX2 down-regulation in the context of amyloidosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined observations of NPTX2 and GluA4 reduction in AD and the mouse model data.

claim: CSF NPTX2 levels were reduced in AD subjects.
source: CSF NPTX2 levels were reduced in AD subjects (Figure 5A and B, and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: CSF NPTX1 and NPTXR levels were also reduced in the same CSF samples.
source: CSF NPTX1 and NPTXR levels were also reduced in the same CSF samples (Figure 5A and B, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5A, B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: NPTXR in CSF was detected in WB as three bands corresponding to full length (60 kDa) and presumed cleavage products at 45 kDa and 30 kDa and all three were reduced in AD CSF.
source: NPTXR in CSF was detected in WB as three bands corresponding to full length (60 kDa) and presumed cleavage products at 45 kDa and 30 kDa and all three were reduced in AD CSF (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: NPTX1 and NPTXR are widely expressed at excitatory synapses.
source: NPTX1 and NPTXR are widely expressed at excitatory synapses (Lee et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The reduction of NPTX1 and NPTXR in CSF despite preserved levels in AD brain suggests that their expression in CSF arises from a discrete source.
source: and their reduction in CSF despite preserved levels in AD brain suggests that their expression in CSF arises from a discrete source.
evidence: This is inferred from the discrepancy between brain and CSF levels.

claim: NPTX1 and NPTX2 in human CSF are disulfide-linked oligomers.
source: We determined that NPTX1 and NPTX2 in human CSF are disulfide-linked oligomers (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A) consistent with their known co-assembly in brain (Xu et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Levels of CSF NPTX1 and NPTXR strongly correlate with CSF NPTX2 in individual samples.
source: Moreover, levels of CSF NPTX1 and NPTXR strongly correlate with CSF NPTX2 in individual samples (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: NPTX2 selectively accumulates on PV-interneurons.
source: Since NPTX2 selectively accumulates on PV-interneurons, we infer this as the major source of NPTX1, NPTX2, and NPTXR in CSF.
evidence: This is supported by prior work cited in the manuscript.

claim: PV-interneurons are inferred as the major source of NPTX1, NPTX2, and NPTXR in CSF.
source: Since NPTX2 selectively accumulates on PV-interneurons, we infer this as the major source of NPTX1, NPTX2, and NPTXR in CSF.
evidence: This is inferred from the selective accumulation of NPTX2 on PV-interneurons and the co-assembly of NPTXs.

claim: NPTX2 assayed by ELISA corresponds closely with levels defined by WB.
source: NPTX2 assayed by ELISA corresponds closely with levels defined by WB. n = 64. Pearson correlation coefficient analysis was performed.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The mean NPTX2 level in control CSF was 1067 pg/ml compared to 296 pg/ml in AD.
source: The mean NPTX2 level in control CSF was 1067 pg/ml compared to 296 pg/ml in AD (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: A second independent set of patient CSF samples confirmed consistency of levels in controls and reduction of NPTX2 in AD.
source: Consistent with current standards to document a new biomarker (Noel-Storr et al., 2014) we screened a second independent set of patient CSF samples by WB and ELISA and confirmed consistency of levels in controls and reduction of NPTX2 in AD (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 4, and Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and ELISA data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: NPTX2 ELISA of samples from patients with MCI demonstrated reduction of NPTX2 compared to controls.
source: NPTX2 ELISA of samples from patients with MCI demonstrated reduction of NPTX2 compared to controls (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The specificity, sensitivity and accuracy of NPTX2 was similar to Aβ42 and superior to tau and p-tau for distinguishing controls from AD.
source: Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis revealed the specificity, sensitivity and accuracy of NPTX2 was similar to Aß42 and superior to tau and p-tau for distinguishing controls from AD (Figure 5G–J).
evidence: This is supported by ROC analysis shown in Figure 5G-J.

claim: A ratio of tau or p-tau divided by NPTX2 showed improved performance in distinguishing controls from AD.
source: A ratio of tau or p-tau divided by NPTX2 showed improved performance (Figure 5K and L).
evidence: This is supported by ROC analysis shown in Figure 5K and L.

claim: NPTX1/2/R levels did not correlate with Aβ42 but did positively correlate with tau and p-tau within individual AD patients.
source: NPTX1/2/R levels did not correlate with Aß42 but did positively correlate with tau and p-tau within individual AD patients (Figure 5—figure supplement 5) and controls (NPTX2 vs tau, r = 0.4625, p=0.0002; NPTX2 vs p-tau, r = 0.3607, p=0.0043, Pearson correlation coefficient analysis).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analyses shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5 and stated in the text.

claim: Tau appearance in CSF may be linked to NPTX2 and PV circuit function.
source: This suggests that tau appearance in CSF may be linked to NPTX2 and PV circuit function, however since they change in opposite directions in AD and yet are positively correlated in both controls and AD their association appears complex.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observed correlations.

claim: The association between tau and NPTX2 in CSF appears complex.
source: This suggests that tau appearance in CSF may be linked to NPTX2 and PV circuit function, however since they change in opposite directions in AD and yet are positively correlated in both controls and AD their association appears complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that they change in opposite directions in AD but are positively correlated.

claim: The complementarity of tau/p-tau and NPTX2 in diagnostic performance suggests they detect distinct processes.
source: Moreover, their complementarity in diagnostic performance suggests they detect distinct processes.
evidence: This is inferred from the improved diagnostic performance of tau/NPTX2 ratios.

claim: NPTX2 levels showed positive correlations (p < 0.05) with the Dementia Rating Scale (DRS).
source: Detailed cognitive data available for the second set of AD subjects revealed positive correlations (p < 0.05) of NPTX2 with the Dementia Rating Scale (DRS) (Mattis, 1988), Digital symbol substitution (Wechsler, 1981), modified Wisconsin Card Sorting Task (Nelson, 1976), Block design Subtest (Wechsler, 1974), Visual Reproduction Test [Russell Adaptation WMS; (Wechsler, 1945), semantic verbal fluency [SVF (Borkowski et al., 1967), California verbal learning test [CVLT (Delis et al., 1987) (Figure 6 and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analyses shown in Figure 6 and Table 1.

claim: NPTX2 levels showed positive correlations (p < 0.05) with Digital symbol substitution.
source: Detailed cognitive data available for the second set of AD subjects revealed positive correlations (p < 0.05) of NPTX2 with the Dementia Rating Scale (DRS) (Mattis, 1988), Digital symbol substitution (Wechsler, 1981), modified Wisconsin Card Sorting Task (Nelson, 1976), Block design Subtest (Wechsler, 1974), Visual Reproduction Test [Russell Adaptation WMS; (Wechsler, 1945), semantic verbal fluency [SVF (Borkowski et al., 1967), California verbal learning test [CVLT (Delis et al., 1987) (Figure 6 and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analyses shown in Table 1.

claim: NPTX2 levels showed positive correlations (p < 0.05) with modified Wisconsin Card Sorting Task.
source: Detailed cognitive data available for the second set of AD subjects revealed positive correlations (p < 0.05) of NPTX2 with the Dementia Rating Scale (DRS) (Mattis, 1988), Digital symbol substitution (Wechsler, 1981), modified Wisconsin Card Sorting Task (Nelson, 1976), Block design Subtest (Wechsler, 1974), Visual Reproduction Test [Russell Adaptation WMS; (Wechsler, 1945), semantic verbal fluency [SVF (Borkowski et al., 1967), California verbal learning test [CVLT (Delis et al., 1987) (Figure 6 and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analyses shown in Figure 6E and Table 1.

claim: NPTX2 levels showed positive correlations (p < 0.05) with Block design Subtest.
source: Detailed cognitive data available for the second set of AD subjects revealed positive correlations (p < 0.05) of NPTX2 with the Dementia Rating Scale (DRS) (Mattis, 1988), Digital symbol substitution (Wechsler, 1981), modified Wisconsin Card Sorting Task (Nelson, 1976), Block design Subtest (Wechsler, 1974), Visual Reproduction Test [Russell Adaptation WMS; (Wechsler, 1945), semantic verbal fluency [SVF (Borkowski et al., 1967), California verbal learning test [CVLT (Delis et al., 1987) (Figure 6 and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analyses shown in Table 1.

claim: NPTX2 levels showed positive correlations (p < 0.05) with Visual Reproduction Test.
source: Detailed cognitive data available for the second set of AD subjects revealed positive correlations (p < 0.05) of NPTX2 with the Dementia Rating Scale (DRS) (Mattis, 1988), Digital symbol substitution (Wechsler, 1981), modified Wisconsin Card Sorting Task (Nelson, 1976), Block design Subtest (Wechsler, 1974), Visual Reproduction Test [Russell Adaptation WMS; (Wechsler, 1945), semantic verbal fluency [SVF (Borkowski et al., 1967), California verbal learning test [CVLT (Delis et al., 1987) (Figure 6 and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analyses shown in Figure 6G and Table 1.

claim: NPTX2 levels showed positive correlations (p < 0.05) with semantic verbal fluency.
source: Detailed cognitive data available for the second set of AD subjects revealed positive correlations (p < 0.05) of NPTX2 with the Dementia Rating Scale (DRS) (Mattis, 1988), Digital symbol substitution (Wechsler, 1981), modified Wisconsin Card Sorting Task (Nelson, 1976), Block design Subtest (Wechsler, 1974), Visual Reproduction Test [Russell Adaptation WMS; (Wechsler, 1945), semantic verbal fluency [SVF (Borkowski et al., 1967), California verbal learning test [CVLT (Delis et al., 1987) (Figure 6 and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analyses shown in Figure 6F and Table 1.

claim: NPTX2 levels showed positive correlations (p < 0.05) with California verbal learning test.
source: Detailed cognitive data available for the second set of AD subjects revealed positive correlations (p < 0.05) of NPTX2 with the Dementia Rating Scale (DRS) (Mattis, 1988), Digital symbol substitution (Wechsler, 1981), modified Wisconsin Card Sorting Task (Nelson, 1976), Block design Subtest (Wechsler, 1974), Visual Reproduction Test [Russell Adaptation WMS; (Wechsler, 1945), semantic verbal fluency [SVF (Borkowski et al., 1967), California verbal learning test [CVLT (Delis et al., 1987) (Figure 6 and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analyses shown in Figure 6H and Table 1.

claim: Aβ42 levels correlated with SVF and CVLT.
source: By contrast, Aß42 levels correlated with SVF and CVLT, while tau and p-tau did not correlate with these behavioral tests (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analyses shown in Table 1.

claim: Tau and p-tau did not correlate with behavioral tests.
source: By contrast, Aß42 levels correlated with SVF and CVLT, while tau and p-tau did not correlate with these behavioral tests (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analyses shown in Table 1.

claim: NPTX2 levels correlated with hippocampal occupancy.
source: NPTX2 levels also correlated with hippocampal occupancy (Heister et al., 2011), a measure of hippocampal volume, while Aß42, tau and p-tau did not (Figure 6I and J, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6J and Table 1.

claim: Aβ42, tau and p-tau did not correlate with hippocampal occupancy.
source: NPTX2 levels also correlated with hippocampal occupancy (Heister et al., 2011), a measure of hippocampal volume, while Aß42, tau and p-tau did not (Figure 6I and J, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analyses shown in Table 1.

claim: Measures of hippocampal volume show robust associations with cognitive performance and AD progression.
source: Measures of hippocampal volume show robust associations with cognitive performance and AD progression (Fjell et al., 2010; Heister et al., 2011; Jack et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: NPTX2 could be an informative biomarker for AD.
source: The observed reductions of NPTX2 protein in human brain and CSF, and the correlation of CSF NPTX2 with cognitive status and hippocampal volume provide support for the notion that NPTX2 could be an informative biomarker for AD.
evidence: This is inferred from the multiple lines of evidence showing NPTX2 reduction and correlations with clinical measures.

claim: NPTX2 appears 'orthogonal' to Aβ and tau.
source: The potential value of NPTX2 as a biomarker is further advanced by the observation that NPTX2 appears 'orthogonal' to Aß and tau since NPTX2 is not reduced as a direct consequence of Aß amyloid in mouse models, appears independent of Aß in human asymptomatic AD (pre AD), and reductions of CSF NPTX2 do not correlate with reduction of CSF Aß42 or increases of tau/p-tau.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple observations showing independence of NPTX2 from Aβ and tau.

claim: CSF levels of NPTX2 might distinguish subjects who will be most responsive to amyloid reducing therapy.
source: Because of the synergistic effects of amyloidosis and NPTX2 down regulation, CSF levels of NPTX2 might distinguish subjects who will be most responsive to amyloid reducing therapy.
evidence: This is speculated based on the synergistic effects observed in the mouse model.

claim: CSF NPTX2 may anticipate disease progression.
source: A recent study reported that CSF NPTX2 may anticipate disease progression (Swanson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: An important proximal cause of cognitive decline in AD is failure of the adaptive function of pyramidal neurons to modify excitatory drive of fast spiking parvalbumin (PV) interneurons.
source: In particular, we propose that an important proximal cause of cognitive decline in AD is failure of the adaptive function of pyramidal neurons to modify excitatory drive of fast spiking parvalbumin (PV) interneurons.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis of the study, supported by multiple lines of evidence.

claim: NPTX2 is expressed in pyramidal neurons as an IEG.
source: The proposed mechanism builds upon prior studies that demonstrate NPTX2 is expressed in pyramidal neurons as an IEG (Tsui et al., 1996)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: NPTX2 is a Ca2+ dependent lectin.
source: NPTX2 is a Ca2+ dependent lectin and appears to bind the glycoprotein network that prominently surrounds PV interneurons (Chang et al., 2010; Tsui et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: NPTX2 appears to bind the glycoprotein network that prominently surrounds PV interneurons.
source: NPTX2 is a Ca2+ dependent lectin and appears to bind the glycoprotein network that prominently surrounds PV interneurons (Chang et al., 2010; Tsui et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: NPTX2 binds to postsynaptic AMPA receptors.
source: NPTX2 also binds to postsynaptic AMPA receptors (Lee et al., 2017; O'Brien et al., 1999; Xu et al., 2003) and acts to increase local accumulation of AMPA receptors and strengthen synapses.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: NPTX2 acts to increase local accumulation of AMPA receptors and strengthen synapses.
source: NPTX2 also binds to postsynaptic AMPA receptors (Lee et al., 2017; O'Brien et al., 1999; Xu et al., 2003) and acts to increase local accumulation of AMPA receptors and strengthen synapses.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Genetic deletion of NPTX2 results in a selective reduction of pyramidal neuron drive of PV interneurons in developing mouse cortex.
source: This action of NPTX2 at excitatory synapses on PV interneurons is evident in vivo where genetic deletion of NPTX2 results in a selective reduction of pyramidal neuron drive of PV interneurons in developing mouse cortex (Gu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Nptx2-/- alone does not result in marked changes of PV interneuron function as assayed by gamma oscillations in vivo or in acute slices.
source: Nptx2-/- alone does not result in marked changes of PV interneuron function as assayed by gamma oscillations in vivo or in acute slices, but Nptx2-/- combined with Nptxr-/- resulted in a profound disruption of gamma oscillations and cognitive deficits in combination with a reduction of GluA4 protein in PV-interneurons (Pelkey et al., 2015, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and data in Figure 3.

claim: Nptx2-/- combined with Nptxr-/- resulted in a profound disruption of gamma oscillations and cognitive deficits in combination with a reduction of GluA4 protein in PV-interneurons.
source: Nptx2-/- alone does not result in marked changes of PV interneuron function as assayed by gamma oscillations in vivo or in acute slices, but Nptx2-/- combined with Nptxr-/- resulted in a profound disruption of gamma oscillations and cognitive deficits in combination with a reduction of GluA4 protein in PV-interneurons (Pelkey et al., 2015, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: GluA4 protein reduction in Nptx2-/-/Nptxr-/- was not associated with a reduced expression of Gria4 mRNA, TARP protein, parvalbumin immunoreactivity, or alteration of the perineuronal glycoprotein network.
source: GluA4 protein reduction was not associated with a reduced expression of Gria4 mRNA, TARP protein, parvalbumin immunoreactivity, or alteration of the perineuronal glycoprotein network.
evidence: This is stated based on prior work.

claim: Presynaptic NPTX2 is required to bind postsynaptic GluA4 and prevent receptor turnover in conditions of altered activity consequent to Nptxr-/-.
source: A hypothetical model was suggested in which presynaptic NPTX2 is required to bind postsynaptic GluA4 and prevent receptor turnover in conditions of altered activity consequent to Nptxr-/- (Pelkey et al., 2015, 2016).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior work.

claim: Amyloid expression (like Nptxr-/-) acts in synergy with Nptx2-/- to down-regulate GluA4 expression.
source: We confirmed in a mouse model that amyloid expression (like Nptxr-/-) acts in synergy with Nptx2-/- to down-regulate GluA4 expression and results in anticipated changes of excitability and rhythmicity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: GluA4 and NPTX2 correlate within samples in both AD cases and in aged controls.
source: Unexpectedly, GluA4 and NPTX2 correlate within samples in both AD cases and in aged controls.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In young adults NPTX2 and GluA4 expression do not appear to correlate within samples.
source: This is notable since in young adults NPTX2 and GluA4 expression do not appear to correlate within samples, and NPTX2 appears higher in young brain than in aged controls.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: NPTX2 appears higher in young brain than in aged controls.
source: This is notable since in young adults NPTX2 and GluA4 expression do not appear to correlate within samples, and NPTX2 appears higher in young brain than in aged controls.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: GluA4 expression in PV interneurons becomes dependent on pyramidal neuron expression of NPTX2 during normal aging.
source: This age-dependence requires further analysis, but suggests that GluA4 expression in PV interneurons becomes dependent on pyramidal neuron expression of NPTX2 during normal aging, and GluA4 expression-PV interneuron function become critically reduced in AD as NPTX2 expression is reduced.
evidence: This is inferred from the age-dependent correlation between NPTX2 and GluA4.

claim: GluA4 expression-PV interneuron function become critically reduced in AD as NPTX2 expression is reduced.
source: This age-dependence requires further analysis, but suggests that GluA4 expression in PV interneurons becomes dependent on pyramidal neuron expression of NPTX2 during normal aging, and GluA4 expression-PV interneuron function become critically reduced in AD as NPTX2 expression is reduced.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined observations of NPTX2 and GluA4 reduction in AD and their correlation.

claim: Amyloid reduces PV interneuron excitability by reducing expression of the voltage sensitive sodium channel Nav1.1.
source: Amyloid reduces PV interneuron excitability by reducing expression of the voltage sensitive sodium channel Nav1.1 (Verret et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: NPTX2 down-regulation reduces pyramidal neuron excitatory drive of PV-interneurons.
source: By contrast, NPTX2 down-regulation reduces pyramidal neuron excitatory drive of PV-interneurons.
evidence: This is based on the known function of NPTX2 and data from the manuscript.

claim: As an IEG, NPTX2 natural expression is dynamic and limited to neurons that engage in information processing such as place cells of the hippocampus.
source: As an IEG, NPTX2 natural expression is dynamic and limited to neurons that engage in information processing such as place cells of the hippocampus [see for example the use of IEGs to detect place cells of the hippocampus (Guzowski et al., 1999; Vazdarjanova et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on IEGs.

claim: NPTX2 expression establishes 'informational' circuits between pyramidal neurons and PV-interneurons that will preferentially support the future activity of specific ensembles of neurons.
source: As a result of normal behavioral experience NPTX2 expression establishes 'informational' circuits between pyramidal neurons and PV-interneurons that will preferentially support the future activity of specific ensembles of neurons, for example, during developmental wiring of the visual cortex (Gu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and the known function of NPTX2.

claim: NPTX2 reduction in AD occurs after accumulation of amyloid and parallels cognitive decline.
source: Since NPTX2 reduction in AD occurs after accumulation of amyloid and parallels cognitive decline, we hypothesize that circuits can adapt to the effects of amyloid if pyramidal neurons are able to maintain circuit-specific expression of NPTX2.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that NPTX2 is not reduced in asymptomatic AD and correlates with cognitive measures.

claim: Circuits can adapt to the effects of amyloid if pyramidal neurons are able to maintain circuit-specific expression of NPTX2.
source: Since NPTX2 reduction in AD occurs after accumulation of amyloid and parallels cognitive decline, we hypothesize that circuits can adapt to the effects of amyloid if pyramidal neurons are able to maintain circuit-specific expression of NPTX2.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that NPTX2 is not reduced in asymptomatic AD.

claim: NPTX2 down-regulation is a 'second hit' for pyramidal neuron PV-interneuron circuit dysfunction and cognitive failure in AD.
source: This model suggests that NPTX2 down-regulation is a 'second hit' for pyramidal neuron PV-interneuron circuit dysfunction and cognitive failure in AD.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis of the study, supported by multiple lines of evidence.

claim: NPTX2 expression may be considered a resilience factor.
source: Reciprocally, NPTX2 expression may be considered a resilience factor.
evidence: This is inferred from the hypothesis that maintaining NPTX2 allows adaptation to amyloid.

claim: The combined action of amyloidosis and NPTX2 down-regulation will produce a disruption of the dynamic recruitment of pyramidal neuron-PV interneuron circuits.
source: Our model predicts that the combined action of amyloidosis and NPTX2 down-regulation will produce a disruption of the dynamic recruitment of pyramidal neuron-PV interneuron circuits.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the proposed model.

claim: Brain activity is reportedly increased in MCI, early AD and aged controls in regions termed the 'default network'.
source: Consistent with these predictions brain activity is reportedly increased in MCI, early AD and aged controls in regions termed the 'default network' (Buckner et al., 2005; Greicius et al., 2004; Sperling et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Dynamic connectivity within and between different resting state networks measured by fMRI blood oxygen level dependent (BOLD) signals is reduced in AD.
source: and dynamic connectivity within and between different resting state networks measured by fMRI blood oxygen level dependent (BOLD) signals is reduced in AD (Thomas et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The capacity for gamma rhythmicity is thought to underlie dynamic connectivity.
source: Since the capacity for gamma rhythmicity is thought to underlie dynamic connectivity (Buzsáki and Wang, 2012; Engel et al., 2001), reduced fMRI BOLD signals may be the imaging correlate of dysfunctional pyramidal neuron-PV interneuron circuits.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Reduced fMRI BOLD signals may be the imaging correlate of dysfunctional pyramidal neuron-PV interneuron circuits.
source: Since the capacity for gamma rhythmicity is thought to underlie dynamic connectivity (Buzsáki and Wang, 2012; Engel et al., 2001), reduced fMRI BOLD signals may be the imaging correlate of dysfunctional pyramidal neuron-PV interneuron circuits.
evidence: This is inferred from the link between gamma rhythmicity and dynamic connectivity.

claim: Deficits of gamma oscillations are associated with cognitive impairment in human cognitive disease including AD.
source: Deficits of gamma oscillations are associated with cognitive impairment in human cognitive disease including AD (Basar, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Both NPTX2 down-regulation and fMRI functional connectivity similarly correlate with clinical Dementia Rating scores.
source: It is further notable that both NPTX2 down-regulation and fMRI functional connectivity similarly correlate with clinical Dementia Rating scores (Thomas et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and data from the current study.

claim: The failure of dynamic circuit properties is most consequential for cognitive dysfunction in AD.
source: Accordingly, we hypothesize that the failure of dynamic circuit properties is most consequential for cognitive dysfunction in AD.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the multiple lines of evidence presented.

claim: Increased activity consequent to amyloid and NPTX2 reduction might accelerate disease progression by placing increased demand on alternative homeostatic mechanisms that weaken pyramidal neuron excitatory synapses, including Arc and Homer1a.
source: Independent of NPTX2's role in forming 'informational' circuits, increased activity consequent to amyloid and NPTX2 reduction migh accelerate disease progression by placing increased demand on alternative homeostatic mechanisms that weaken pyramidal neuron excitatory synapses, including Arc (Shepherd et al., 2006) and Homer1a (Hu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on known homeostatic mechanisms.

claim: The homeostatic mechanism mediated by Arc generates Aβ by enhancing secretase processing of APP.
source: Notably, the homeostatic mechanism mediated by Arc generates Aß by enhancing secretase processing of APP (Wu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Arc is induced by Aβ activation of metabotropic glutamate receptors.
source: A feed-forward mechanism of synaptic weakening is suggested by the observation that Arc is induced by Aß activation of metabotropic glutamate receptors (Um et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Arc is reported to drive synapse elimination in the developing cerebellum.
source: Arc is reported to drive synapse elimination in the developing cerebellum (Mikuni et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: If Arc's action is increased consequent to amyloid and failure of pyramidal neuron-NPTX2-GluA4 homeostasis it could contribute to increased Aβ generation as well as weakening and loss of excitatory synapses on pyramidal neurons.
source: If Arc's action is increased consequent to amyloid and failure of pyramidal neuron-NPTX2-GluA4 homeostasis it could contribute to increased Aß generation as well as weakening and loss of excitatory synapses on pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the known functions of Arc.
